Headline: Asbestos concerns prompt Tokmanni to issue warning about 'Stretcherz' toys
Full_Text: Some of the toys may contain asbestos, a dangerous carcinogen. Finnish department store chain Tokmanni has issued a warning to consumers that some 'Stretcherz'-branded toys it has sold may contain asbestos. UK toy manufacturer HTI issued a product safety recall regarding the affected sand-filled toys on 13 February. The toys have been sold at Tokmanni and other stores in Finland. The recall affects some, but not all, of the firm's Stretcherz-branded product line. Tokmanni said that the toys can be returned to the place of purchase for a refund. Headline: EV registrations up by 22%; petrol and diesel share falls
Full_Text: Nearly 60 percent of all last year's new cars were rechargeable, with less than 40 percent petrol-powered and just four percent diesel-powered. The number of new vehicle registrations in Finland has been declining year by year in the 2020s, and 2025 was another lacklustre year. Fewer than 72,000 new passenger cars were registered, three percent less than the year before. The number was the lowest figure so far in this century, Statistics Finland said on Friday. Imports of used vehicles decreased by four percent in 2025, totalling just over 41,000. The largest numbers were brought in from Sweden and Germany. Meanwhile the number of new trucks and busses on the road fell by 15 and 25 percent respectively. Last year, 37 percent of new passenger cars were fully electric cars, an increase of 22 percent from the year before. Meanwhile consumers shied away from plug-in hybrids, with new registrations slipping by two percent. Overall, the number of plug-in passenger cars rose by 12 percent from 2024. Meanwhile registrations of new petrol- and diesel-powered cars both fell by nearly one-fifth. Nearly 60 percent of all new cars were rechargeable, with less than 40 percent petrol-powered and just four percent diesel-powered. Headline: At least 15k customers in limbo after ordering from bankruptcy-hit Asko, Sotka
Full_Text: Up to 20,000 customers are still waiting for goods they ordered from the home furnishing chains before the bankruptcy filing. At least 15,000 customers who bought items from home furnishing companies Asko and Sotka will not receive those goods because the firms' owner recently filed for bankruptcy, news agency STT reports. The chains' owner, Indoor Group, filed for bankruptcy earlier this month. According to the firm's bankruptcy estate administrator, Tuomas Penttilä, up to 20,000 customers are still waiting for goods they ordered from the home furnishing chains before the bankruptcy filing. At least 15,000 of them will not likely receive the items, Penttilä told STT, noting that those customers have paid in full, or at least partially, for the items. If a product has been marked as sold to a particular customer, then it is likely it will still be delivered. According to Penttilä, this is the case for about 1,000 to 2,000 of the orders on file. Headline: Finnish police use new law to launch first probes into suspected FGM cases, paper says
Full_Text: Finland introduced a specific law banning the practice and preparation of female genital mutilation (FGM) at the beginning of last year. Police in different parts of Finland have launched separate preliminary investigations into suspected cases of female genital mutilation (FGM). The investigations are the first of their kind, according to Helsingin Sanomat, since a specific law banning the practice and preparation of FGM was introduced at the beginning of 2025. Previously, FGM was only punishable under law as assault or aggravated assault. According to Helsingin Sanomat's information, the first investigation is taking place in the Kuopio region, where police suspect the mutilation has already occurred. In a separate case, police in Tampere have investigated suspicions that a woman or girl was being prepared for an FGM procedure. Although the exact details of the case are not currently known, this could mean the victim is being forced or coerced into being mutilated, or they are being taken abroad for the purpose of having the procedure carried out. Both acts are now illegal under Finnish law. Finland's Minister of Education, Anders Adlercreutz (SPP), said earlier this year that he wants to investigate whether girls are being taken out of the country to undergo FMG procedures, and to see how common the practice might be. His comments followed an Yle investigation which uncovered evidence that some Somali parents in Finland have sent their children to disciplinary institutions in Somalia. Once there, the report revealed, they are subjected to severe treatment — including physical abuse and being locked in chains. Headline: Finland aims to outlaw unauthorised possession, import of radio signal jammers
Full_Text: Incidents of suspected GPS interference have risen sharply in Finland over recent years, especially around airports and in the Baltic Sea region. Finland's government wants to legislate against the unauthorised possession and import of devices intended for deliberate radio interference, commonly known as jammers. The proposal relates to equipment that jam or spoof radio communications networks, such as GPS. In a press release, the Ministry of Transport and Communications noted that unauthorised use of the devices is already banned under Finnish law, but this proposed amendment would allow for their confiscation. "Criminalising the unauthorised possession of jammers would improve the authorities’ possibilities to intervene in the unauthorised possession and import of such devices," the press release said. The number of incidents of suspected GPS interference has risen sharply in Finland over recent years, especially around airports and in the Gulf of Finland. Headline: Helsinki Metro services suspended following incident on track
Full_Text: A man was seriously injured after being trapped under a Metro train. The Helsinki Metro line was suspended between Helsinki University and Ruoholahti for about an hour on Wednesday morning following an incident on the tracks. According to reports in the immediate aftermath of the incident, a person suffered a serious injury in the vicinity of the Helsinki Central Station. Several units from the Helsinki Rescue Department were dispatched to the scene shortly after 10am. The department confirmed to reporters about 20 minutes later that a casualty had occurred, and that responsibility for providing further information about the incident would be passed to Helsinki police. Helsingin Sanomat reported on Wednesday afternoon, citing a statement from Helsinki police, that an adult male was seriously injured after becoming trapped under a Metro train.
